history.contentOut: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) is a geoengineering technique that involves the injection of aerosols into the stratosphere to reflect sunlight, thereby mimicking the cooling effects of major volcanic eruptions, such as that of Mount Pinatubo. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) recognizes SAI as one of the most-studied geoengineering approaches. While research initiatives, including those at Harvard, propose small-scale testing of SAI, concerns remain regarding its long-term implications. It is essential to distinguish between actual mitigation strategies and proposed geoengineering solutions, as reliance on temporary fixes may detract from comprehensive climate action.

Tide gauges and satellite altimetry show that global mean sea level (GMSL) rose during the 20th century and has accelerated in recent decades. IPCC AR6 assesses that GMSL rose faster since 1900 than over any preceding century in at least 3,000 years, with the rate for 2006–2018 higher than the 20th-century average. The two largest contributions are ocean thermal expansion as the ocean takes up heat, and meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets. Local relative sea level can differ because of land subsidence or uplift, ocean dynamics, and gravitational fingerprints of ice loss. A floating iceberg melting in a glass of water does not raise the water line much (Archimedes); that classroom demo does not apply to grounded ice sheets on land adding mass to the ocean. Sea-level rise did occur after the last ice age, but the recent acceleration is linked to anthropogenic warming, not a claim that the ocean was static before factories. Coastal flooding risk increases even when the global rate is millimetres per year because extremes sit on a higher baseline.
history.contentOut: Global mean sea level (GMSL) has risen throughout the 20th century, with an acceleration observed in recent decades. The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) indicates that GMSL has increased more rapidly since 1900 than in any other century over the past 3,000 years. The average rate of GMSL rise from 2006 to 2018 exceeded that of the 20th century. The primary contributors to this rise are ocean thermal expansion due to heat absorption and meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets. Local sea level variations can occur due to factors such as land subsidence, uplift, ocean dynamics, and the gravitational effects of ice loss. It is important to note that while melting floating ice does not significantly raise sea level, the melting of grounded ice sheets contributes mass to the ocean. Although sea-level rise has occurred since the last ice age, the recent acceleration is primarily attributed to anthropogenic warming, highlighting the increasing risk of coastal flooding even at a global rise measured in millimeters per year.
